title: Transfusion reaction
banner: DRAFT, NOT clinically reviewed. Fictional scenario specification; never imported, published or shown to learners.
learning_objectives: Recognise a possible transfusion reaction and stop the transfusion.
Keep access and inform the prescriber and the transfusion service.
Record and hand over the event factually.
Recognise that further treatment is a prescriber decision.

setting: A fictional adult receiving a blood component on a fictional unit.

steps.info: Twenty minutes into a transfusion, an adult develops fever and shivering. The component is still infusing. The patient was not shivering at the previous check; the cause of the new symptoms and the current circulatory status are not yet established.
steps.prompt: Which immediate response best addresses a suspected serious transfusion reaction while preserving the component for investigation?

options.text: Stop the transfusion immediately; assess patient/vitals, notify team and blood bank, verify identity. Maintain IV access without flushing implicated blood; preserve product/set per policy. Do not independently restart.
options.feedback: An ISBT educational module supports stopping the transfusion when a reaction is suspected, urgent clinical reassessment, patient/component identity checks and immediate blood-bank notification. Maintaining venous access must not mean flushing blood remaining in the implicated transfusion tubing into the patient. The product and set should be retained for investigation as instructed; further treatment and any decision about restarting require specialist/team assessment. For suspected serious reactions do not restart the implicated component. For other reactions any resumption requires a satisfactory specialist/team assessment and local protocol; never restart independently. Activate emergency response immediately for compromised airway, breathing or circulation. Fever with rigors can represent a serious reaction, including bacterial contamination or acute haemolysis. Do not presume a benign febrile reaction or restart the component; obtain urgent clinical and transfusion-service assessment. BSH 2023 severe-reaction guidance supports disconnecting and retaining the implicated set and component while maintaining venous access with suitable separate saline equipment according to the local transfusion pathway. This case concerns suspected serious reaction, not hemorrhage-associated hypotension in which interruption decisions require immediate expert assessment.
options.consequence: Stopping the implicated component, assessing the patient and notifying the team may limit further exposure and support urgent investigation.

options.text: Reduce the transfusion rate, record the temperature and symptoms, repeat observations in an hour and keep the component running while waiting to determine whether the findings settle or require notification of the blood bank.
options.feedback: Slowing the transfusion is unsafe when a reaction may be developing; stop it while the patient is assessed and the clinical/transfusion team is notified.
options.consequence: Slowing instead of stopping could prolong exposure during a serious reaction.

options.text: Treat the fever with a medicine selected independently from ward stock, continue the transfusion and monitor the temperature and symptoms; notify the clinical team only if the fever persists after medication and further observations.
options.feedback: Medicines need an order, and the transfusion should be stopped first.
options.consequence: Treating fever while continuing the component could delay recognition of a serious reaction.

steps.info: At the final shared checkpoint, the implicated transfusion is stopped and the clinician is present. Rigors continue, temperature has risen from the earlier reading and blood pressure is falling. Laboratory investigation is not yet complete; venous access has been maintained.
steps.prompt: What is the priority when circulation worsens after the component has been stopped?

observations.label: Transfusion-service investigation
observations.value: Coordinate ordered tests; do not wait for results

observations.label: Implicated component and set
observations.value: Retain as directed; do not restart

options.text: Escalate falling pressure immediately; reassess ABC, report transfusion timeline and identity, preserve product/set and coordinate ordered investigations with the transfusion service.
options.feedback: Fever, rigors and circulatory deterioration can indicate a severe acute transfusion reaction, including bacterial contamination or acute haemolysis. Do not restart. Activate emergency support and coordinate the clinician-directed work-up, including cultures or haemolysis investigations if ordered. Do not delay resuscitation to complete paperwork. BSH emphasizes that emergency management is guided by clinical severity and must not wait for laboratory results. For severe dyspnea, the team assesses potential anaphylaxis, pulmonary edema and transfusion-associated lung injury; respiratory symptoms alone do not establish TACO or TRALI. TACO may become apparent during transfusion or up to 12 hours afterwards; TRALI typically develops during transfusion or within six hours of completion. These are recognition windows, not a reason to dismiss later deterioration. Do not assume fluid overload or give a diuretic reflexively. Suspected anaphylaxis requires emergency help and prompt intramuscular adrenaline (epinephrine) through the authorised anaphylaxis pathway; do not delay urgent treatment for investigations.
options.consequence: Emergency support and a clear clinical timeline may allow investigation of serious causes without delaying resuscitation.

options.text: Report only that the patient seemed well earlier, without reconstructing the transfusion timeline or providing component details, and leave the remaining assessment and investigation coordination to the next clinician.
options.feedback: An incomplete account loses the timeline of the reaction.
options.consequence: An incomplete report could obscure the sequence and severity of the reaction.

options.text: Use the symptoms and falling pressure to decide the reaction type, recommend treatment to the doctor and defer emergency escalation until the cause has been established.
options.feedback: Recognize and report possible serious causes, but diagnosis and treatment selection require the responsible team; do not delay emergency support.
options.consequence: Prematurely assigning a reaction type could delay urgent assessment and appropriate treatment.

learning_points: Stop the transfusion and inform the team and transfusion service at the first sign of a reaction.
Keep intravenous access; further treatment is a prescriber decision.
Give and record a factual timeline: component and estimated volume infused, transfusion start and stop times, symptom onset, changes from baseline vital signs, and the response to initial actions.
Do not independently restart a transfusion following a suspected reaction; activate emergency response for compromised airway, breathing or circulation.
Fever with rigors or hypotension requires urgent evaluation for serious causes such as bacterial contamination or acute haemolysis; do not restart the implicated component.
Clinical severity determines urgency; coordinate investigations in parallel with emergency treatment, and preserve the implicated component and giving set according to the transfusion service.

TACO may become apparent during transfusion or up to 12 hours afterwards; TRALI typically develops during transfusion or within six hours of completion. These are recognition windows, not a reason to dismiss later deterioration. Do not assume fluid overload or give a diuretic reflexively.
Suspected anaphylaxis requires emergency help and prompt intramuscular adrenaline (epinephrine) through the authorised anaphylaxis pathway; do not delay urgent treatment for investigations.
